edits.walkthrough_append: **EXAM TRAP:** Raw material sourcing weighs QUALITY, COST, and CONTINUITY together — choosing the cheapest supplier who cannot deliver on time fails the continuity test; and just-in-time buying lowers storage cost but transfers stock-out risk to the supplier relationship, a trade-off the case question is built on.

**EXAM TRAP:** Plant layout arranges MACHINES, product layout arranges the production LINE for one standardised product, and fixed-position layout keeps the PRODUCT stationary while resources move to it — misclassifying shipbuilding (fixed-position) as plant layout, or claiming one layout suits all firms, loses the classification mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** Statutory compliance is PRE-OPERATIVE — registration, licences, and tax registrations must exist BEFORE opening; and compliance is CONTINUOUS (returns, renewals, records), not a one-time gate — describing it as a single registration step misses both the sequence and the ongoing duty.

**EXAM TRAP:** Operational risk arises FROM WITHIN the business process — machine breakdown, process failure, human error — distinguishing it from market risk (prices) and credit risk (counterparties); and the response ladder runs avoid → reduce → transfer (insurance) → accept, matched to impact and probability, which is exactly what the case tests.

**EXAM TRAP:** Environmental risk is EXTERNAL in origin but manageable in IMPACT — floods or regulation changes cannot be prevented by the firm, yet siting, insurance, and contingency planning reduce exposure; writing "nothing can be done about natural risks" conflates uncontrollable origin with uncontrollable consequence and loses the mitigation mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** Credit risk is the COUNTERPARTY'S failure to pay — not the bank's own liquidity shortage — and banks manage it through credit appraisal, collateral, and provisioning (NPA classification); describing a run on deposits as credit risk confuses funding risk with lending risk, the distinction the question isolates.

**EXAM TRAP:** Internal causes — poor management, overtrading, cash-flow mismanagement, fraud — are SELF-INFLICTED and largely controllable; external causes (recession, policy shock) are not; attributing failure to "bad luck" while ignoring working-capital indiscipline misses precisely the controllability distinction the question rewards.

**EXAM TRAP:** Insurance TRANSFERS the financial sting but requires PREMIUM payment and covers only insurable, fortuitous losses — deliberate damage and wear-and-tear are never covered; and transfer (insurance) differs from avoidance (drop the activity) — answering "the firm avoids the risk by insuring it" mixes the two responses.

**EXAM TRAP:** The three levels are TOP (strategic, long-term, whole-organisation), MIDDLE (tactical, departmental, medium-term), and OPERATIONAL/LOWER (day-to-day, task-level) — authority DECREASES and detail INCREASES going down; reversing which level sets strategy, or giving operational examples for strategic decisions, loses the level marks.

**EXAM TRAP:** The monitor role GATHERS information from inside and outside the organisation — it is the INPUT step that feeds the disseminator (passing information inward-down) and spokesperson (outward); describing the monitor as "reporting to the press" confuses the three informational roles and loses the differentiation mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** The figurehead role is CEREMONIAL and SYMBOLIC (signing documents, greeting dignitaries) — it involves no decision-making and no interpersonal leadership of subordinates; attributing motivation of employees (the leader role) or negotiation (decisional role) to the figurehead confuses Mintzberg's clusters.

**EXAM TRAP:** The disturbance handler REACTS to crises the organisation did not choose (strike, supplier collapse), while the entrepreneur role PROACTIVELY initiates change — a manager doing both is not contradictory, but examiners award the mark only when the reactive-versus-proactive distinction is explicit.

**EXAM TRAP:** Delegation passes AUTHORITY and RESPONSIBILITY downward but ACCOUNTABILITY cannot be delegated — the manager remains answerable for outcomes; writing "the manager is freed of accountability once work is delegated" inverts the principle and loses the delegation mark instantly.

**EXAM TRAP:** Decentralisation is the SYSTEMATIC dispersal of decision authority across levels — broader than delegation, which is a single manager-task relationship — and neither means abdication: top management retains policy control; equating decentralisation with delegation or with dilution of accountability misses the conceptual hierarchy.

**EXAM TRAP:** External forces (technology, competition, regulation, social shifts) originate outside; internal forces (new leadership, workforce expectations, process drift) inside — and change is SUCCESSFUL only when both are diagnosed, since an internally resisted change fails regardless of external logic; attributing all change pressure to competition alone loses the two-force analysis.

**EXAM TRAP:** ADKAR is SEQUENTIAL — Awareness and Desire come before Knowledge and Ability, with Reinforcement last — skipping to training (Knowledge) before building Desire produces skilled resisters; answering with the five words as an unordered list loses the sequencing logic that makes ADKAR a change checklist.

**EXAM TRAP:** A passbook kiosk automates ROUTINE ledger printing so clerks shift to advisory work — productivity gains come from OFFLOADING volume, not from faster clerks; and the machine prints, it does not UPDATE passbooks offline (entries originate in the core banking system); missing the redeployment logic loses the productivity-analysis mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** Barcode scanning converts light reflection into a product CODE — the code fetches price and description from the database, so the scanner itself never "knows" prices; and barcodes identify PRODUCTS, not weighables (loose vegetables need weighing scales) — the code-versus-price confusion is the standard mark-loser.

**EXAM TRAP:** A POS terminal records the sale, computes GST, updates INVENTORY in real time, and prints the receipt in one action — the inventory update is automatic because the sale triggers it, not a separate step; describing stock update as a manual end-of-day task defeats the POS's integration purpose.

**EXAM TRAP:** Biometric authentication verifies WHO YOU ARE from body traits (fingerprint, iris, face) versus cards (what you have) and PINs (what you know) — traits cannot be forgotten or stolen but CANNOT be changed if compromised; the possession-knowledge-inherence triad is exactly what the comparison question scores.

**EXAM TRAP:** VoIP PACKETISES voice and transmits it over data networks — cutting call cost by bypassing the telephone company's circuit — but quality depends on bandwidth and latency, an emergency call may fail without power, and numbering/location tracing is harder; writing "VoIP is just cheaper, with no drawbacks" misses the trade-off half of the answer.

**EXAM TRAP:** Wi-Fi provides MOBILITY and eliminates cabling cost, but its range is limited and signals need WPA security — open networks invite interception; answering "Wi-Fi is faster than wired" is factually wrong for matched standards, and the productivity case rests on flexibility, not raw speed.

**EXAM TRAP:** Self check-in kiosks shift ROUTINE check-in from staff to passengers, freeing agents for bags, irregular operations, and premium service — productivity rises through TASK REALLOCATION, not only through speed; and passengers with special needs still need counters, which is why kiosks supplement rather than replace desks.

**EXAM TRAP:** CUTE (Common Use Terminal Equipment) lets ANY airline's check-in run on ANY shared workstation by connecting to a central platform — each airline keeps its own host system behind a common interface; describing CUTE as one airline's proprietary system inverts the shared-infrastructure idea and loses the airport-productivity mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** An airport operational system SYNCHRONISES flights, gates, baggage, and resources on one live picture — the productivity gain is cross-system coordination, not any single automation; and when one flight is delayed, the system re-allocates gates and baggage belts downstream — that ripple-management, not data entry, is the answer's core.

**EXAM TRAP:** HRM is PERVASIVE (every manager manages people), CONTINUOUS, DYNAMIC, and STRATEGIC — not a clerical personnel function; and it manages PEOPLE as resources who think and feel, unlike machines — writing HRM as "recruitment and salary work only" truncates the concept and loses the characteristics marks.

**EXAM TRAP:** HRM functions span the EMPLOYEE LIFECYCLE — procurement (recruitment, selection), development (training, appraisal), compensation (wages, incentives), integration, maintenance, and separation — and each function serves BOTH organisational goals and employee needs; listing only recruitment shows a lifecycle gap that costs half the marks.

**EXAM TRAP:** Campus recruitment offers FRESH talent at scale with lower per-hire cost, but hires are UNTESTED in real work and need induction investment — and campus offers typically carry a service-bond or joining-delay issue; answering only the advantages when the question says "merits and demerits" forfeits half the marks.

**EXAM TRAP:** The medical test screens FITNESS FOR THE JOB — eyesight for drivers, stamina for field work — not general health; it comes AFTER selection decision but BEFORE appointment, and rejecting on a non-job-related condition (disability unrelated to duties) raises discrimination issues, which is the applied nuance the case tests.

**EXAM TRAP:** Induction is SOCIALISATION, not orientation paperwork alone — it converts a stranger into an aligned member by communicating culture, colleagues, and expectations in the first weeks; and its cost of neglect is early attrition: writing induction as a one-day HR formality loses the socialisation half of the answer.

**EXAM TRAP:** Refresher training UPDATES existing skills (new machinery, revised law, software versions) — the employee already knows the fundamentals — whereas vestibule training uses a simulated workplace and apprenticeship combines earning with learning; matching the training type to the employee's experience level is where the classification mark sits.

**EXAM TRAP:** Classroom training delivers UNIFORM theory to many at low per-head cost with expert faculty — but it is off-the-job, so skills transfer to the workplace is imperfect and interaction is one-to-many; writing "classroom training is always best because experts teach" ignores the transfer gap that the method-comparison question targets.

**EXAM TRAP:** Morale is INVISIBLE and DYNAMIC — inferred from behaviour (turnover, absenteeism, grievances), not measured directly — and it is GROUP-oriented, not merely individual happiness; writing "morale means satisfaction" conflates a shared climate with a personal feeling, the conceptual slip the definition question screens for.

**EXAM TRAP:** Stimulants (recognition, participation, fair pay, growth) and depressants (autocracy, favouritism, unsafe conditions) act on the SAME morale climate — and money alone is a short-lived stimulant if fairness is absent; answering with a one-sided list when the question asks for BOTH directions loses half the marks.

**EXAM TRAP:** Motivation is INTERNAL and GOAL-DIRECTED — needs create tension, tension drives behaviour toward goals, and satisfaction of one need releases the drive for the next (the process, not just the word); describing motivation as "giving bonuses" confuses the incentive (external) with the motive (internal state).

**EXAM TRAP:** Monetary incentives satisfy SURVIVAL and security needs; non-monetary incentives (recognition, autonomy, growth) feed esteem and self-actualisation — and the mix must match the employee's need level, since money stops motivating once basic needs are met; answering "higher pay always motivates more" ignores the need-hierarchy logic the question tests.

**EXAM TRAP:** Laissez-faire works ONLY with highly skilled, self-motivated teams — with junior or unaligned members it collapses into abdication and drift; and the leader still remains ACCOUNTABLE for outcomes; writing "the leader does nothing" or recommending the style universally misses both the conditionality and the retained responsibility.

**EXAM TRAP:** The continuum (Tannenbaum-Schmidt) runs boss-centred to subordinate-centred, and the EFFECTIVE leader SLIDES along it based on the situation — subordinates' readiness, time pressure, and the importance of the decision; declaring one fixed best style anywhere on the continuum is precisely the answer the continuum was drawn to refute.

**EXAM TRAP:** Situational leadership matches STYLE to the FOLLOWER's readiness — telling for low readiness, selling for moderate, participating for high, delegating for very high — and the same leader uses different styles with different subordinates; recommending delegating to novices (or telling to experts) inverts the readiness-style match.

**EXAM TRAP:** The Blake-Mouton grid scores CONCERN FOR PRODUCTION against CONCERN FOR PEOPLE — 9,9 team management is the ideal, 1,1 impoverished, 9,1 task/authority, 1,9 country club — and MIDDLE-OF-THE-ROAD (5,5) is balance, not excellence; mixing up 9,1 and 1,9 is the classic grid-question slip.

**EXAM TRAP:** A dry promotion raises the TITLE without upgrading job content, authority, or pay — its usual purpose is retaining an employee when no pay budget exists; and because duties stay the same, dissatisfaction often follows; answering "a dry promotion is a normal promotion" misses the mismatch that the term exists to name.

**EXAM TRAP:** Seniority-based promotion is OBJECTIVE and dispute-free but rewards AGE, not merit — it can entrench mediocrity and demotivate high performers; merit-based promotion is performance-true but needs tamper-proof appraisal; the standard answer names BOTH systems' trade-offs and the seniority-cum-merit compromise, not one pole alone.

**EXAM TRAP:** Compulsory retirement is RULE-TRIGGERED (reaching the specified age), voluntary retirement is EMPLOYEE-CHOSEN (usually with VRS compensation), and both differ from retrenchment, which is EMPLOYER-initiated for surplus staff — mixing VRS (employee option) with retrenchment (employer decision) is the standard separation-mode error.

**EXAM TRAP:** In resignation the EMPLOYEE initiates separation; in dismissal the EMPLOYER does, for misconduct after due inquiry — and a resignation usually needs NOTICE or notice-pay while dismissal can forfeit benefits; writing "resignation and dismissal are both employer decisions" inverts the initiative that defines each mode.

**EXAM TRAP:** Flexible hours anchor a FIXED CORE period for meetings and collaboration around which employees shift start/end times — total daily hours stay constant; flextime differs from compressed weeks (fewer, longer days) and from remote work (location), and conflating the three arrangements is the standard classification slip.

**EXAM TRAP:** WFH shifts work OUTSIDE the office using digital tools — its benefits (commute savings, focus, talent reach) pair with risks (isolation, supervision difficulty, data security) — and it is a LOCATION arrangement, distinct from flextime (timing); answering with benefits alone when the question invites both sides loses half the marks.

**EXAM TRAP:** Written communication creates a PERMANENT, verifiable, time-stamped record and suits complex, formal, or distant communication — but it is slow, delayed, and offers no immediate feedback; and "more words" is not its strength — PRECISION is; answering with speed as a merit inverts the medium's actual trade-off.

**EXAM TRAP:** Gestures can CONFIRM, CONTRADICT, or REPLACE speech — crossed arms may contradict a spoken "yes," and a nod can replace words entirely — but gestures are CULTURE-BOUND (a nod or thumbs-up differs across cultures); reading body language as universal truth is precisely the misinterpretation the question is set to catch.

**EXAM TRAP:** Physical-mechanical barriers live in the TRANSMISSION MEDIUM — noise, faulty equipment, poor network, illegible writing, distance — while semantic barriers live in WORDS and psychological ones in MINDS; filing "noise in the sender's thinking" under physical (it is psychological) blurs the taxonomy the classification question tests.

**EXAM TRAP:** Socio-psychological barriers are MENTAL FILTERS — premature evaluation, lack of trust, emotions, status block, selective perception — inside the communicators themselves; and they operate at BOTH ends (sender's fear, receiver's bias), not just the receiver's; answering with only one side loses the two-way analysis mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** The appointment letter is the CONTRACT that follows the offer letter — it converts the verbal offer into enforceable terms (role, pay, hours, notice period, confidentiality) and is issued AFTER acceptance and document verification; treating the interview offer as the binding document inverts the sequence and loses the contractual-stage mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** Globalisation's five attributes — interconnectedness, liberalisation, borderless-ness, integration, and technology-driving — REINFORCE each other, so removing liberalisation (tariff walls) weakens integration; and globalisation is a PROCESS, not an end state; listing attributes without their mutual reinforcement misses the synthesis the question asks for.

**EXAM TRAP:** The service provider DELIVERS the outsourced service under a formal contract with SLAs — it is an OUTSIDER, not a department, and the outsourcing FIRM remains accountable to its customers; writing "responsibility transfers fully to the provider" ignores retained accountability, the governance point the question tests.

**EXAM TRAP:** BPO segments follow SKILL: front-office (customer-facing), back-office (processing, payroll), and KPO (knowledge-intensive analytics, research) — KPO demands professional expertise and delivers higher value; filing data-entry under KPO, or calling all outsourcing IT services, misclassifies the tiers the question separates.

**EXAM TRAP:** Intra-B is ELECTRONIC EXCHANGE WITHIN one firm — department-to-department data flow and workflow automation on the company's own network — distinct from B2B (between firms) and B2C (to consumers); giving a supplier-portal example for Intra-B confuses internal integration with external commerce and loses the classification mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** A packer is the LAST regulated entity before the consumer — its duties include FSSAI licence display, ingredient and allergen labelling, net quantity, batch and expiry details — and labelling law holds the packer liable even for manufacturer defaults; naming the packer as "just a wrapper" misses the legal responsibility the question targets.

**EXAM TRAP:** Investment is EXPENDITURE ON NEW CAPITAL GOODS (machines, buildings, inventories) — buying existing shares is a transfer of ownership, not investment in the national-income sense; and induced investment responds to income while autonomous investment does not — the share-purchase slip is the standard macro-definition mark-loser.

**EXAM TRAP:** Income is a FLOW over a period (per month, per year), while wealth is a STOCK at a point in time — mixing the two units in national-income questions loses the measurement mark; and transfer incomes (pensions, gifts) are excluded from factor income because they match no productive service.

**EXAM TRAP:** The business cycle's phases run peak → recession → trough → recovery in ORDER, and each phase feeds the next through demand, investment, and expectations — a decline in GDP growth RATE is not recession (the level must CONTRACT); and no single phase is permanent, which is the point the cycle diagram rewards.

**EXAM TRAP:** Equilibrium price and output sit where AD equals AS — above it, unplanned inventory build-up signals producers to cut output; below it, inventory depletion signals expansion — quoting the intersection without the inventory-adjustment mechanism answers only half the macro question.
